title: Information from social ties predicts conspiracy beliefs: Evidence from the attempted assassination of Donald Trump
screen_reason: US survey (n = 2,765, 17-21 July 2024, days after the 13 July assassination attempt) reporting the share of respondents who had HEARD each of two conspiracy theories about the event: 41% the right-leaning 'Democratic operatives planned it' theory, 53% the left-leaning 'it was staged' theory. Those are shares of survey respondents reporting encounter with a specific false narrative, i.e. RECALL (exposure) under §1. The paper's aim is a belief model, but the awareness shares are reported descriptively (Fig. 1) and qualify the paper under the 'aim is something else' rule.

estimates.platform: online survey; exposure is not tied to a platform (respondents could have heard it anywhere)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who had heard the right-leaning conspiracy theory that the Trump shooting was planned by Democratic operatives
estimates.value_raw: 41% of n = 2,765 respondents; belief-model subsample of those who had heard it, n = 1,081
estimates.denominator: 2,765 US adults, online nonprobability sample with quotas for gender, race, age and region (PureSpectrum), poststratified to US Census demographics, NCHS urbanicity and FEC 2020 turnout/vote choice
estimates.definition: respondent reported having heard the conspiracy theory that the shooting was planned by Democratic operatives aiming to prevent Trump from winning the 2024 election
estimates.misinfo_def: "conspiracy theories—that is, attempts to explain the causes of events through secret plots by powerful actors"
estimates.source_quote: A total of 41% had heard the right-leaning conspiracy theory that the shooting was planned by Democratic operatives.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 2; Fig. 1 'Percent respondents who reported awareness and belief in the conspiracy theories emerging after the attempted assassination of Donald Trump'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report: respondents said whether they had heard the narrative. IMPORTANT NUANCE - the veracity/conspiracy status of the two narratives is fixed by the authors, not by the respondent: both are treated as conspiracy theories under the Douglas et al. definition and are documented as such in the press fact-checks the paper cites (CBS News on the Trump rally shooting conspiracy theories; AP fact-check showing the photograph used to support the 'staged' claim was taken in 2022, before Trump's ear was injured). ground_truth is coded self_report per the schema rule for RECALL. The authors argue recall is comparatively reliable here because the event was singular and only days old, citing Guess et al. 2019 and Tourangeau et al. 2000, and they note the 'social media' response option conflates content from social ties, strangers and news media.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data were collected via an online nonprobability sample with quotas for gender, race, age, and region. Respondents (n=2,765) were recruited by the panel sample vendor PureSpectrum between 2024 July 17 and 21.
estimates.notes: Two rows, not one range row, because the two theories are substantively different narratives with opposite political valence that the paper analyses separately throughout (separate logistic regressions, separate belief subsamples). DENOMINATOR CHECK worth an adjudicator's eye: the belief subsample is n = 1,081, which is 39.1% of 2,765, against a reported 41%; the gap is consistent with the poststratification weights being applied to the reported percentage. It is not stated explicitly whether the awareness question was asked of everyone or only of the 95% who knew about the assassination attempt; if the latter, the true denominator is about 2,627 and the figure would be a share of the aware.

estimates.platform: online survey; exposure is not tied to a platform (respondents could have heard it anywhere)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who had heard the left-leaning conspiracy theory that the assassination attempt was staged and not real
estimates.value_raw: 53% of n = 2,765 respondents; belief-model subsample of those who had heard it, n = 1,348
estimates.denominator: 2,765 US adults, online nonprobability sample with quotas for gender, race, age and region (PureSpectrum), poststratified to US Census demographics, NCHS urbanicity and FEC 2020 turnout/vote choice
estimates.definition: respondent reported having heard the conspiracy theory that the assassination attempt was staged by Republican political actors and not real
estimates.misinfo_def: "conspiracy theories—that is, attempts to explain the causes of events through secret plots by powerful actors"
estimates.source_quote: Over half of the respondents (53%) were aware of the left- leaning conspiracy theory that the attempted assassination was staged and not real.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report: respondents said whether they had heard the narrative. IMPORTANT NUANCE - the veracity/conspiracy status of the two narratives is fixed by the authors, not by the respondent: both are treated as conspiracy theories under the Douglas et al. definition and are documented as such in the press fact-checks the paper cites (CBS News on the Trump rally shooting conspiracy theories; AP fact-check showing the photograph used to support the 'staged' claim was taken in 2022, before Trump's ear was injured). ground_truth is coded self_report per the schema rule for RECALL. The authors argue recall is comparatively reliable here because the event was singular and only days old, citing Guess et al. 2019 and Tourangeau et al. 2000, and they note the 'social media' response option conflates content from social ties, strangers and news media.
estimates.moderator_quote: We measured self-reported information consumption by asking people who knew of the Trump assassination attempt where they obtained information about it. Respondents selected all applicable answers from eight options including people I know, television, social media, and news websites.
estimates.notes: Same denominator caveat as the paired row: n = 1,348 in the belief subsample is 48.8% of 2,765 against a reported 53%, consistent with weighting; and it is not stated whether the awareness item was asked of all respondents or only of the 95% aware of the event. This narrative is the more widely encountered of the two despite being the left-leaning one, which is a useful counterweight to the usual right-skew finding and is worth preserving in the coding. On the source_quote: 'left- leaning' with a space reproduces a line-break hyphenation artifact in the extracted text; the printed sentence reads 'left-leaning'.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and deliberately NOT extracted: (1) '95%' of respondents were aware of the assassination attempt itself — awareness of a real event, not of misinformation. (2) Information sources for the event overall among those aware: television 64%, social media 43%, interpersonal social networks 30% — channel use, not misinformation exposure. (3) Sources of each conspiracy theory AMONG THOSE WHO HEARD IT: right-leaning theory, social media 53%, interpersonal 32%, television 28%; left-leaning theory, social media 52%, interpersonal 34%, television 21%. These are compositions of the already-exposed subgroup, not population prevalence, and the paper's own footnote says they sum to more than 100% because respondents could pick multiple sources. Multiplying them by the awareness rates to get a population-level 'heard it on social media' share would be a computed cross-category product, forbidden by R8 — though an adjudicator should note that 41% x 53% and 53% x 52% would put social-media-sourced exposure at roughly a fifth to a quarter of the adult population for each theory. (4) All belief figures: 13% 'very likely' plus 16% 'somewhat likely' for the right-leaning theory, 12% plus 17% for the left-leaning one, each among those who had heard it, summarised by the authors as 'close to a third'. Belief in false claims is explicitly excluded by §1, and the summed values would in any case be a forbidden cross-category sum. (5) Regression results (Figs 3-4, Tables S1-S6) and the '0.2-0.4 increase on a 0-4 scale' effect of interpersonal ties — effect sizes, not prevalence; the authors themselves 'urge caution in generalizing precise point estimates'. NOTE: the Supporting Information (survey item text, descriptive statistics, sample details) is referenced repeatedly but is not in this text file, so the exact awareness item wording could not be checked; if the SI is available it would settle the denominator question raised in both rows.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, 17-21 July 2024, four to eight days after the 13 July 2024 event. Online NONPROBABILITY sample from panel vendor PureSpectrum with quotas for gender, race, age and region; n = 2,765; no response rate is calculable. Poststratification weights built from US Census race/ethnicity, age, gender, education and region, NCHS urban-rural classification, interlocking gender-by-age-by-race, education-by-age and education-by-race cells, and FEC 2020 turnout and vote choice. IRB-approved (Rochester STU00219054), online informed consent. Exposure and belief both self-reported; the authors defend recall accuracy on grounds of topic specificity and event recency, and note that the 'social media' response option conflates content from social ties, strangers and news media. Belief measured 0-4 on a likelihood rather than agree-disagree format to reduce acquiescence. Belief regressions run on the exposed subsamples (n = 1,081 right-leaning; n = 1,348 left-leaning). No coding of content and hence no intercoder reliability. Replication materials at OSF doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/5RHTN. Author-stated limits: no causal claims, belief strength/certainty not measured, generalisability to other events unknown.
rob.item6_quote: Almost immediately after the event, conspiracy theories—that is, attempts to explain the causes of events through secret plots by powerful actors (3)—emerged on both sides of the political spectrum.
rob.item10_quote: A total of 41% had heard the right-leaning conspiracy theory that the shooting was planned by Democratic operatives. ... Over half of the respondents (53%) were aware of the left-leaning conspiracy theory that the attempted assassination was staged and not real.
